title: Granular Synthesis — rich
forward_vector: I am the manifest of Granular Synthesis's rich face: three walks that test the page's own sentences on its own equations (what a grain is and whether a cloud's color is its grain's; whether grains pile where the filter is; whether a bent cloud tunes itself), and the neighbours' pieces gathered where they answer this page's questions. I hold the fingerprint of the words each piece was made against, and the offers the pieces taught the text, waiting for Loudon. I never hold the entry's words.

pieces.title: is the cloud's color the grain's? · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption:
**One grain, then a cloud, then the opening sentence measured.** A sine grain whose length decides click or note (length × width stays near 2 for the Hann window); the window that decides how much it clicks (side lobes −13, −31, −56 dB; Gabor's Δt·Δf 0.58, 0.082, 0.080 against the floor 1 ⁄ 4π); a cloud whose density decides how much it fuses. The test sets three clouds against one grain's prediction (Campbell's theorem, no free knob): random onsets land on it within about 1 dB, at one pitch or an octave of them, and a hundred times the density only lifts the level 20 dB. The same grains on a regular clock miss by 46 to 57 dB: a comb of lines at the rate, a pitch no grain carries.

P(f) = λ · |G(f)|²

(the cloud's power at each frequency) = (grains a second) × (one grain's own power there)

verdicts.file: Granular Synthesis — rich — atom and material.html
verdicts.why: A real test that walks up from one grain: random onsets land on one grain's prediction (0.66–1.29 dB) and clocked onsets miss it (46–57 dB), all reproduced. Advised: scope the verdict's 'the atom sets the color' and 'texture, not timbre' to identical, independent grains and the long-term spectrum, since a spread cloud's color is the population's pitch distribution.

pieces.title: do grains pile up where the filter is? · a walk in four steps
pieces.caption:
**The hybrid built and played.** One grain caught or not by one partial (Adler's rule: caught when its detuning is under the pull, else it beats at √(Δ² − pull²), checked at 15 settings); a loud well and a shallow one, whose catchments come out 30 and 10.6 Hz against the rule's 30 and 9 (the loud partial below drags grains near the quiet one a hertz or two); the whole spectrum under a bandpass you drag. The test: partial by partial, the share of grains caught follows the filtered amplitude within about 0.03 of the rule, wherever the filter sits. And a knob the section never names: at K ⁄ 2π = 30 Hz the lone-partial rule says 0.55 of grains are caught; 1000 ms grains reach 0.51, 300 ms 0.41, 60 ms 0.15, 15 ms 0.03. A grain must live long enough to be caught.

dθᵢ⁄dt = ωᵢ + Σₖ Aₖ · K · sin(Θₖ − θᵢ)

(how fast grain i's phase turns) = (its own speed) + the sum over partials of (the partial's filtered loudness) × (the pull) × sin(the partial's phase − the grain's)

verdicts.why: The pile-follows-filter test holds (0.012 / 0.031), but the grain-length sweep blames the 0.6 Hz yardstick on the physics: a lone Adler partial is caught at 0.469 / 0.555 / 0.552 at 60 / 120 / 300 ms, and the engine reads 0.361 / 0.480 / 0.515 at 2 Hz, because the neighbouring partials wobble locked grains. Measure caught by phase slip (or show the 2 Hz row and the lone-partial ceiling), rewrite the verdict, caption and offer 2 from it, and name the 2/T-against-catchment point for grains under about 30 ms.

pieces.title: does a bent cloud tune itself? · a walk in six steps
pieces.caption:
**The three regimes, one pull at a time, and the boldest sentence measured.** No pull; the partials pulling (with wells apart, 49% of grains caught, every one by its nearest partial; with wells overlapping, 57% caught and 13% of those by a louder partial further off); one pile whose grains hear each other (already phase-locked at no grain-to-grain pull, r = 0.78 ≈ π ⁄ 4, rising to 0.92 at 40 Hz); grains hearing only each other, which group 1 : 1. Then the feedback bent: a soft clip locks a stray at 3 × a choir and never at 2 ×; a lopsided bend locks 2 ×. The test, six random clouds per bend: straight 0 of 6 grew a harmonic, soft clip 0 of 6, lopsided 4 of 6 in Node (15 grains at 2 ×, 4 at 3 × the group that formed) and 3 of 6 in Chromium (1 and 7): the clouds are chaotic, so the same seeds part ways in the last bits between engines, and the split moves while the answer doesn't. The grain-to-grain coupling goes through the analytic signal of the cloud's bent sound; the lopsided bend's DC and difference tones are left out.

+ K_g · Re( Y · e^(−iθᵢ) ),  Y = the analytic signal of G(u)

(the cloud's own sound, bent by G, pulling each grain at the frequencies it holds)

verdicts.why: Steps 3–6 are sound and step 6 is a real test (soft 0/6, lopsided 4/6, control 0/6). Step 2's caught meter shares capture's yardstick: 57% at K_A 80 is 79% at 2 Hz and 92% by the lone rule, while the nearest share (87–88%) is robust. Use the same phase measure, re-read step 2 and the caption, trim offer 5's 'many find none', and say 'reach past the midpoint' for 'overlapping'.

pieces.title: two clouds meet · 7 s
pieces.caption: **Collision and merging, heard.** Two fountains of grains aimed at each other, 72 grains, the aim tightening from 6° to 0.15°: 13 clacks in the air, 119 of 360 landings by a deflected grain. From [[Particle Synthesis]]'s face, where it is still a proposal.

pieces.title: the same clouds, passing through · 7 s
pieces.caption: The same 72 grains at the same gain with collisions off: rain, no meetings. Set beside the one above, it is the bullet's claim as an A ⁄ B: in a particle system the meeting happens by rule, not by a crossfade.

verdicts.why: It makes the collision bullet heard against a same-gain control, and its numbers (13 meetings, 119 of 360) match the source.
The control that makes the pair an A/B. Caption note: B is collisions off, not the bullet's crossfade, so 'not by a crossfade' claims a little more than the pair shows.

pieces.title: how many grains make a color? · from Neural Granular Synthesis
pieces.caption: **The minimum grain count, and density against coupling, on a neighbour's crowd.** Not the attractor hybrid, but the same two questions on a crowd of coupled grains: uncoupled, the crowd's gappiness comes within about a fifth of steady noise from about 32 grains firing six times a second; locked, it stays five to six times the floor at every size from 4 to 512. A dense cloud that locks does lose its motion into a pulse. From [[Neural Granular Synthesis]]'s face, where it is still a proposal. For the hybrid itself, the capture walk above found the attractor's catch does not depend on how many grains there are (8 grains or 48, at 300 ms: 0.43 and 0.41 caught), since each grain feels only the partials.

verdicts.file: /Projects/Neural Granular Synthesis/Neural Granular Synthesis — rich — crowd-size ladder.html
verdicts.why: Gathered, tracked, conform-clean, and the caption says it is not the hybrid. Note: 'a dense cloud that locks' uses Neural's onset lock, not this page's carrier-phase lock; write 'a crowd whose firings lock'.

offers.what: 'whose collective statistical behavior produces emergent timbres': measured on the atom-and-material walk, a cloud at random onsets has exactly its grain's color raised by the density (Campbell's theorem; measured spectrum within 0.7 to 1.3 dB of one grain's prediction at 10 ms and 40 ms Hann, 100 ms Gauss and 40 ms rectangle grains, one pitch or an octave of them; density ×100 lifts the level 20.4 to 20.8 dB and leaves the shape within 1.1 dB). What emerges is texture, and, when onsets fall on a clock, a pitch no grain carries (regular onsets miss the prediction by 46 to 57 dB, a comb at the rate). Suggested, if Loudon's ear agrees: '…whose collective statistics produce emergent textures — and, when the onsets keep time, pitches no grain carries; the color itself is the grain's, raised by the density.'

The section never names grain length, and the capture walk finds it decides whether the attractor is heard. With the filter open and K ⁄ 2π = 30 Hz, the share of grains caught is 0.026 at 15 ms, 0.066 at 30, 0.148 at 60, 0.257 at 120, 0.414 at 300 and 0.511 at 1000 ms, against Adler's 0.545 for a lone partial and a grain that lives forever (the neighbouring partials, 110 Hz away, narrow each well a little). Suggested addition after 'Grains pile up where the filter is, scatter where it isn't.': 'Only grains that live long enough are caught: catching takes about 1 ⁄ (A_k·K) and several times that, so short grains drift past whatever the filter does.'

Name K's unit and the capture rule the equation implies: with K in rad ⁄ s, a grain is caught by partial k when it starts within A_k·K ⁄ 2π Hz of it (Adler's rule). The capture walk's step 1 checks it at 15 settings (caught below the line; beats at √(Δ² − (A·K ⁄ 2π)²) above it, within 6%).

'Computationally efficient: … N_grains × N_partials evaluations': the same sum costs N_grains + N_partials. Since sin(Θ_k − θ_i) = Im(e^{iΘ_k} e^{−iθ_i}), Σ_k A_k sin(Θ_k − θ_i) = Im(X · e^{−iθ_i}) with X = Σ_k A_k e^{iΘ_k} computed once per sample; the capture and three-regimes engines compute the page's exact equation this way. Suggested: '(coupling is one-directional, and the attractor's pull on every grain comes from one sum over the partials per sample: N_grains + N_partials evaluations, no grain-to-grain interactions).'

'Each grain independently finds its nearest attractor partial': measured on the three-regimes engine (harmonics of 110 Hz, the even ones loud, the odd at a quarter; 400 ms grains born 165 to 1375 Hz), with the wells apart (K ⁄ 2π = 40 Hz at full loudness) 49% of grains are caught, every one by its nearest partial; with the wells overlapping (80 Hz), 57% are caught and 13% of those by a louder partial further off. Suggested: 'Each grain is caught by a partial whose pull, A_k·K, outruns its detuning — usually the nearest, sometimes a louder one further off, and none at all if it sits between wells.'

'Weak grain-to-grain coupling added: … Each pile becomes coherent — not just a frequency cluster but a phase-locked cluster': at no grain-to-grain pull a pile is already phase-locked to its partial, each caught grain at its own fixed offset (sin φ = Δ ⁄ (A·K ⁄ 2π)), fanned so the pile's coherence is r = 0.782 against π ⁄ 4 = 0.785 predicted (one partial at 440 Hz, 24 grains born within 42 Hz, pull 30 Hz). Grain-to-grain coupling closes the fan and pulls edge grains in: r 0.795, 0.832, 0.919, 0.960 and caught 87%, 99%, 99%, 99% at K_g ⁄ 2π = 10, 20, 40, 80 Hz (73% at 0). Suggested: 'Each pile, already locked to its partial but fanned across phase offsets, closes ranks: its grains come into step with each other, and grains at its edges are pulled in.'

'Add soft clipping or any nonlinearity, and harmonic locking appears. The cloud self-organizes into a harmonic series that nobody specified.' Measured on the three-regimes engine, with the cloud's sound bent by G before the grains hear it (soft clip tanh(Du) ⁄ D; lopsided, the same with a bias; both slope 1 at zero; drive 3). Placed by hand 1.5 Hz sharp or flat of 2 × and 3 × a ten-grain choir at 220 Hz (K_g ⁄ 2π = 40 Hz): the soft clip locks the 3 × stray and never the 2 ×; the lopsided bend locks the 2 ×; straight, neither. Six random clouds per bend (64 grains, 110 to 880 Hz, K_g ⁄ 2π = 250 Hz): straight 0 of 6 grew a harmonic, soft clip 0 of 6 (its groups smaller, 10.7 grains against 19.5, since its pull stops growing as a group gets loud), lopsided 4 of 6 in Node, with 15 grains at 2 × and 4 at 3 × a group that formed on its own (3 of 6 in Chromium, 1 and 7: the clouds are chaotic and the same seeds part ways between engines). Suggested: 'Bend the feedback and harmonic locking becomes possible: a symmetric soft clip holds only odd ratios, 3 : 1; a lopsided bend holds even ones too, 2 : 1. Grains near a harmonic of a group lock to it, and with a lopsided bend a random cloud grows the start of a harmonic series nobody specified.' The model leaves out the lopsided bend's DC and difference tones.
